title: Diagnostic Trainer
subtitle: Practice cases as in real life: find the abnormality on an image, work through lab results, take a virtual patient to a diagnosis. Accuracy earns points and rank.

whatLabs: Work through a lab panel: what matters, what is secondary
whatVp: Take a history, order tests, reach a diagnosis

radiology.name: Imaging
radiology.t1: Find the abnormalities on the image and point to each one with the mouse — the marker goes where you see the pathology.
radiology.t2: Name every finding from the palette and complete the review protocol area by area.
radiology.t3: Write the impression in your own words and state the diagnosis.
radiology.ai: Most of the score here comes from something you cannot forward to an outside model: the finding must be located and marked ON THE IMAGE, in its own coordinates. A screenshot sent to a chatbot comes back as a description in words, not as annotations.

labs.name: Lab results
labs.t1: Go through the panel and flag the values whose deviation is clinically significant.
labs.t2: Out of reference range and clinically significant are not the same thing; the second is what is scored.
labs.t3: Write the interpretation and state the diagnosis.
labs.ai: On this station the data is text, and forwarding it anywhere is technically easy. Something else works here: the exam time limit, and the fact that the score rests on picking out what matters, not on elegant wording.

vp.name: Virtual patient
vp.t1: Read the complaint and history and record a working differential — before any investigations.
vp.t2: Order investigations one at a time: a result is revealed only after it is ordered, and every order is recorded.
vp.t3: State the final diagnosis and justify it.
vp.ai: The working diagnosis is named from a single complaint, with no results yet — on that input an outside model helps very little. After that what is scored is the path: what you ordered and what you did not. A ready-made diagnosis from elsewhere does not replace that.

rules.scoreH: How the score is made up
rules.scoreNote: If a component does not apply to the case (for example, the author set no diagnosis), it is dropped from the calculation entirely rather than dragging the score down. A case is passed from {{threshold}}.
rules.modesH: Two modes, and they do different things
rules.learn1: No time limit, no limit on attempts.
rules.learn2: AI is openly allowed: ask a chatbot, compare, work through it — that is a normal way to learn.
rules.learn3: No XP is awarded; rank and leaderboard do not change.
rules.learn4: The case average is unaffected by practice.
rules.learn5: The review queue does not move.
rules.learn6: Your daily streak does count — practice keeps it alive.
rules.exam1: Time limit — {{limit}}, counted on the server from the moment the attempt starts.
rules.exam1NoLimit: The time limit is counted on the server from the moment the attempt starts.
rules.exam2: One graded attempt per case every {{hours}} h.
rules.exam3: No hints, and pasting text into the answer fields is disabled.
rules.exam4: XP, rank, leaderboard, achievements and case statistics come only from here.
rules.exam5: A weak result puts the case into the review queue.
rules.exam6: We assume the answers are your own: the point of a graded attempt is to measure your knowledge, not a chatbot's availability.
rules.outcome1: The first graded attempt at a case — full XP, the case counts as completed, and it is this attempt that sets the case average.
rules.outcome2: A repeat graded attempt (once {{hours}} h have passed) — {{share}}% of the usual XP: improving your result is worth it, farming points on cases you already know is mostly not. It no longer changes the case average.
rules.outcome3: Practice — zero XP and no effect on any of the numbers. The review afterwards is still complete, with the author's reference answer.
rules.outcome4: Your best result on the case is kept and shown on this screen before your next attempt.
rules.againH: Can you take this case again
rules.again1: Yes. In practice mode — right away and as often as you like, with a full review.
rules.again2: For a grade — {{hours}} h after the previous graded attempt began. The pause is not a punishment: repeating right after the review trains your memory of that one case, whereas a day later it trains clinical reasoning.
rules.again3: A case you did poorly on comes back on its own for review: first after a day, then after three, then after a week. Pass it confidently at the last step and it leaves the queue.
rules.again4: This case has numeric variants ({{count}} data sets including the main one): on a repeat run the numbers will differ while the diagnosis stays the same. So an answer copied from a colleague may not fit — a different value will be the significant one.
rules.time1: Close the tab and come back within the limit — you continue the same attempt on the same timer, and no answers are lost.
rules.time2: An abandoned graded attempt burns along with the slot: the {{hours}} h countdown runs from when it started. Otherwise a graded attempt could be cancelled at will — start, see a hard case, never submit, and call it “not counted”.
rules.time3: A submission after the limit is still accepted — you get your score and the review — but it stops counting towards the grade: otherwise the limit would be decorative.
rules.time4: Practice has no limit at all, and you can interrupt it however you like.
rules.ai1: In practice mode AI is allowed. In a graded attempt we count on your own answer.
rules.ai2: During a graded attempt we record: time spent on the case, text pasted into fields, time spent away from the tab, and how closely your text matches the author's reference answer or a typical chatbot answer to this case.
rules.ai3: These flags do not change your score and block nothing. The case author sees them as “worth a look” — no conclusion is drawn from a single signal, they are far too easily explained by ordinary work.
rules.ai4: We do not use proctoring, do not turn on your camera and do not watch your screen. And we know no browser will ever see the phone next to you: the task is built so that an outside hint simply does not help much.
